title: Storyboards, Scripts & Work Plans
description: How storyboards, scripts and work plans are used to plan moving-image, audio and time-based media projects.
content_html:
Planning Moving-Image and Audio Products

When a media product involves movement, speech or sound unfolding over time — such as a video, animation or podcast — a visualisation diagram is not enough. Creators need documents that capture sequence, timing and sound. The three key planning documents for time-based products are storyboards, scripts and work plans. Together these documents ensure that a complex, multi-stage production stays focused on the original brief throughout the entire process.

Storyboards

A storyboard is a sequence of drawn frames, arranged like a comic strip, that maps out a moving-image or animated product shot by shot. Each frame represents a single shot or scene change, and the space around each frame is used for annotations. A typical storyboard frame includes: a sketch of what the camera will see; a note of the camera angle and shot type (e.g. close-up, wide shot, bird's-eye view); the duration of the shot in seconds; a description of any camera movement (pan, tilt, zoom); the transition to the next shot (cut, dissolve, fade); and notes on the audio — dialogue, voiceover, music or sound effects.

Key Fact

A storyboard frame should include: a sketch of the scene; the shot type and camera angle; the duration of the shot; any camera movement; the transition to the next shot; and audio notes including dialogue, music and sound effects. All six elements should be present for a complete storyboard.

Storyboards are used for videos, animations, advertisements and any other moving-image product. They allow the creator to spot problems — such as a sequence of shots that will be confusing for the viewer, or a scene that requires props or locations that are unavailable — before any filming or animation begins. A well-drawn storyboard also helps when working with a team, because each person can see exactly what is needed for every shot without relying on spoken instructions.

Shot types describe the distance between the camera and the subject: an extreme close-up fills the frame with a single feature (such as an eye); a close-up shows the face; a medium shot shows the upper body; a wide shot shows the full subject in their environment; and an extreme wide shot establishes a location. Camera angles describe the vertical position of the camera: a low angle looks up at the subject and makes them appear powerful; a high angle looks down and makes them appear small or vulnerable; a bird's-eye view is directly overhead; and a worm's-eye view is directly below, looking up. Knowing these terms allows a creator to annotate storyboard frames precisely and communicate their intentions clearly to a filming team or animator.

Scripts

A script is the written plan for the words and sounds in an audio or video production. A video script typically shows dialogue or voiceover on one side of the page alongside a brief description of the matching visuals, so that audio and visual elements can be produced in sync. A radio or podcast script focuses entirely on the spoken content and sound effects, including instructions such as “fade in music” or “pause for two seconds”. Scripts are essential for any production involving speech because they ensure the content is accurate, on-message and the right length before recording begins. A client reviewing a script can check the tone and message without needing to watch a rough cut.

A production script for a video typically includes: the speaker's name before each line of dialogue; descriptions of any narration or voiceover; sound effect and music cues (e.g. “SFX: door slam” or “Music: upbeat track fades in”); scene headings indicating location and time of day; and stage directions describing what is happening on screen. A radio or podcast script follows a similar structure but replaces visual descriptions with timing notes. The script should be formatted clearly so that any performer or technician can follow it without needing to ask questions.

Work Plans and Production Schedules

A work plan (also called a production schedule) is a time-management document. It breaks the entire project down into individual tasks, assigns a deadline and a responsible person to each task, and lists the resources required for each stage. A work plan for a video project might include tasks such as: write script (Day 1-2); film location footage (Day 3-4); record voiceover (Day 5); edit footage (Day 6-8); export and review (Day 9); submit (Day 10). Milestones — key points by which a significant stage must be complete — are often highlighted separately within the plan.

Key Fact

A work plan should always include contingency time: a buffer period built into the schedule to allow for unexpected problems such as equipment failure, illness or a scene that needs to be reshot. Without contingency, any delay will cause the final deadline to be missed. Good planning anticipates problems rather than ignoring them.

Work plans are particularly important when working to a client deadline, as they make it possible to see at a glance whether the project is on track. They also help when resources must be shared — for example, if a camera is only available for two days, the work plan ensures that filming is scheduled within that window. A realistic work plan considers not only how long each task will take in ideal conditions, but also includes time for review, client feedback and final corrections before submission.
exam_tip_html: If an exam question asks you to describe a storyboard, always include detail about what is annotated on each frame — shot type, camera angle, duration, transition and audio notes. Saying ‘it shows what each scene looks like’ alone will score only 1 mark. For work plan questions, remember that contingency is a required element: a plan without built-in buffer time is incomplete. If the question gives a scenario with a tight deadline, always mention contingency as part of your answer, even for lower-mark questions.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Storyboards plan moving-image and animated products shot by shot, with each frame annotated with shot type, camera angle, duration, transitions, camera movement and audio notes.
  • Scripts set out the spoken words, sound effects and music cues for audio and video productions, ensuring content is accurate and the right length before any recording takes place.
  • Work plans break a project into tasks with deadlines, milestones and responsible persons, and must always include contingency time to protect the final deadline against unexpected delays.

glossary_terms.definition: A grid of drawn frames showing each shot in a moving-image or animated product, including camera angles, character positions, dialogue, transitions and timing.
The type of shot used in a storyboard frame, describing the camera's distance from and angle to the subject, such as close-up, wide shot, or bird's-eye view.
A written document that sets out the spoken words, sound effects and music cues for an audio or video product, formatted so that performers and production crew can follow it.
A document that lists all the tasks needed to complete a media project, assigns each task a deadline and responsible person, and identifies the resources required, including time for contingency.

practice_questions.text:
Which pre-production document is most appropriate for planning an animated short film?
A) Visualisation diagram
B) Mood board
C) Storyboard
D) Mind map
State two pieces of information that should be included in a storyboard frame annotation.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: shot type; camera angle; duration / timing of the shot; camera movement (pan, tilt, zoom); transition to the next shot (cut, dissolve, fade); audio notes (dialogue, voiceover, music, sound effects). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a work plan should include contingency time.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Simple point (1 mark): e.g. 'in case something goes wrong'. Development (2 marks): e.g. 'contingency is buffer time built into the schedule to allow for unexpected problems such as equipment failure or the need to reshoot a scene'. Further development (3 marks): e.g. add 'without contingency, any single delay will cause all subsequent tasks to slip, making it impossible to meet the final client deadline, which could damage the creator's professional reputation'. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what a script includes for an audio-visual production, and give one example of how it helps during the production process.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): a script sets out the spoken dialogue or voiceover word for word, alongside sound effect cues, music instructions and visual descriptions, formatted so performers and crew can follow it (2 marks for a clear, developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement). Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a client reviewing the script before filming begins can check that the product's message and tone match the brief, meaning any changes can be made on paper rather than after footage has been recorded (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague reference). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student is producing a 90-second promotional video for a local business. The student has written a script but has not yet produced a storyboard or work plan.

Discuss whether the script alone is sufficient planning for this project.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion identifying what the script provides (accurate dialogue, correct length, client-approved message before filming) alongside what it lacks (no visual plan for each shot, so the student does not know what shots to film or in what order; no time management, so there is no way to ensure the product is ready by the deadline). Argues convincingly that a storyboard is also needed to plan the visual sequence and a work plan to manage the production timeline. Both sides developed with reasoning applied to the 90-second video scenario. Secure (3-4 marks): At least two relevant points identified and briefly explained with some scenario reference. Developing (2 marks): One or two points but without clear explanation. Emerging (1 mark): A single basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A media production company has been commissioned to create a two-minute animated advertisement. The lead animator wants to skip the storyboarding stage to save time.

Evaluate the extent to which storyboarding is essential to the successful completion of this project.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8 marks): A sustained evaluation arguing that storyboarding is highly valuable for animation specifically because: every frame must be drawn from scratch (unlike live action, there is no camera improvisation), so errors discovered mid-animation are very costly to fix; the storyboard allows the client to approve the visual narrative before a single frame is animated; and it coordinates the team so that each animator works on the correct scenes in the correct order. Counter-argument: an experienced solo animator working on a simple product might argue that a rough sketch suffices and a full storyboard is time-consuming. However, for a commissioned, client-facing advertisement, the risks of skipping storyboarding outweigh the time saved. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached. Secure (5-6 marks): Both sides explained with application to animation and some judgement. Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided or surface-level. Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which element must every storyboard frame annotation include to indicate how long the shot lasts on screen?
What term describes the pre-production document that lists all project tasks with deadlines, responsible persons and required resources?
A storyboard frame should annotate the _____ to the next shot, such as a cut, dissolve or fade.
A work plan should always include _____ time: a buffer period built into the schedule to handle unexpected problems.
Match each pre-production document to the product type it is most commonly used to plan.
right: Any audio or video production needing spoken dialogue or narration
Any project requiring task-by-task time management and milestones
An animated short film or promotional video

flashcard_questions.q: What does each frame of a storyboard represent?
flashcard_questions.a: A single shot or scene change in the moving-image product.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a camera angle note in a storyboard?
flashcard_questions.a: A description of the camera's position relative to the subject, such as high angle or bird's-eye view.

flashcard_questions.q: What transition indicates one shot immediately replacing another with no effect?
What does a script set out for an audio or video production?
flashcard_questions.a: Spoken words, sound effects and music cues, formatted for performers and crew.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is a script reviewed by the client before filming begins?
flashcard_questions.a: To check the message and tone match the brief before any footage is recorded.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a milestone in a work plan?
flashcard_questions.a: A key point by which a significant stage of the project must be complete.

flashcard_questions.q: What is contingency time in a work plan?
flashcard_questions.a: A buffer period built in to handle unexpected problems without missing the deadline.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are storyboards especially important when working in a team?
flashcard_questions.a: Each person can see exactly what is needed for every shot without relying on spoken instructions.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a 'dissolve' transition look like between two shots?
flashcard_questions.a: One shot gradually fades into the next rather than cutting abruptly.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a low-angle camera shot suggest about the subject?
flashcard_questions.a: The subject appears powerful or dominant.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the document that breaks a media project into tasks with deadlines and resource requirements.
flashcard_questions.a: A work plan or production schedule.

flashcard_questions.q: For which type of product is a storyboard used rather than a visualisation diagram?
flashcard_questions.a: Moving-image or animated products such as videos and animations.

hero_image_caption: Storyboards, scripts and work plans are the pre-production tools that keep complex moving-image and audio projects on track from the first idea to the final deadline.
